author: sol
stem: A stranger treats the reversed course of a hob as the route direction. Compared with collapsed cairns, how did this error affect misroutings among strangers?

options.text: It caused more misroutings, since strangers usually set aside cairns they recognise as collapsed.
It caused fewer misroutings, since strangers usually trust collapsed cairns as route markers.
options.misreading: A reader who assumes visible damage is still consulted as a route cue would overestimate errors at collapsed cairns.

options.text: It caused similar misroutings, since strangers usually read both reversed and collapsed courses as directions.
options.misreading: A reader who lumps misread hobs together with damaged cairns would miss that strangers ignore obvious collapse.

options.text: It caused fewer misroutings, since strangers usually notice that a reversed course marks a branch.
options.misreading: A reader who transfers trained readers' understanding of hobs to strangers would underrate the Orne effect.

explanation: Under the "Sources of error" heading, the Orne effect accounted for more stranger misroutings than collapsed cairns. Strangers generally recognised collapsed cairns as unreadable and ignored them.

author: sol
stem: A stranger takes the reversed course of a hob as the route direction. If the next cairn is visible, what happens to the frequency of this error?

options.text: It stays about as common, because strangers who choose a direction do not seek confirmation.
It becomes less common, because strangers who see the next cairn check their direction.
options.misreading: A reader who follows Orne's initial expectation would assume a visible next cairn prompts a check.

options.text: It becomes more common, because strangers who see the next cairn mistake it for the branch.
options.misreading: A reader who treats the visible cairn as another confusing signal would infer an added error Orne did not find.

options.text: It stays about as common, because strangers who see the next cairn misread its distant courses.
options.misreading: A reader who remembers equal frequency but attributes it to unreadable distant courses would miss the failure to look for confirmation.

explanation: Under the "When the registers disagree" heading, Orne found the error just as common when the next cairn was visible as when it was not. Once strangers took a direction from a cairn, they did not look for confirmation.

author: sol
stem: Why does the survey protocol measure cant from the crown downward after recording lean?

options.text: The order follows the layout of the original recording sheets, rather than a property of stone.
The order follows the direction in which course offsets accumulate, rather than a recording convention.
options.misreading: A reader who thinks the upper courses determine all lower offsets would mistake a sheet convention for a geometric necessity.

options.text: The order follows the risk of knocking the pell stone loose, rather than a recording convention.
options.misreading: A reader who recalls why pell position is recorded first might apply that reason to the direction of cant measurement.

options.text: The order follows the need to correct frost lean first, rather than a recording convention.
options.misreading: A reader who conflates lean with cant might suppose measuring from the crown helps correct for the whole cairn's tilt.

explanation: Under the "Lean and cant" heading, cant is measured crown downward because that is how Marhaug's printed recording sheets were organised. Nothing in the stone requires that direction.

author: sol
stem: One body course points west between courses that point east both above and below it. For a guild-built cairn, what does that single reversal tell a trained walker?

options.text: A second route branches before the next cairn, while the main route follows the east cants.
The main route turns west at this cairn, while the east cants mark a second route.
options.misreading: A reader who treats the unusual west course as the strongest directional signal would confuse a hob with route direction.

options.text: A second route branches after the next cairn, while the main route follows the east cants.
options.misreading: A reader who recalls that a hob signals a branch but misplaces it would put the junction beyond the next marker.

options.text: The ford becomes high before the next cairn, while the main route follows the east cants toward the pass.
options.misreading: A reader who blends the two registers would read a course reversal as a report about route conditions.

explanation: Under the "The concord index" heading, a hob is one course canted against those above and below it and announces a branch before the next cairn. The worked example shows that the lone reversed course does not change the route direction.

author: sol
stem: A cairn's body courses point east, and its pell stone rests on the downslope side. What two messages should a trained walker take from it?

options.text: The route turns east, while recent walkers reported that the ford was high.
The route turns east, while recent walkers reported that the ford was low.
options.misreading: A reader who reverses the pell stone convention would treat a downslope position as a low-water report.

options.text: The route turns west, while recent walkers reported that the ford was high.
options.misreading: A reader who reads cant as pointing back along the incoming route would reverse the directional message while keeping the pell report.

options.text: The route turns west, while recent walkers reported that the ford was low.
options.misreading: A reader who reverses both the cant direction and the pell convention would invert both registers.

explanation: Under the "Two registers" heading, the courses carry the route direction and the pell stone carries recent ford condition. East cants indicate an east turn; a downslope pell stone means the water was not low.
